clinicalPearls: An episodic syndrome that may be associated with migraine (ICHD-3), affecting mainly school-age children (peak around 5-10 years) and a recognised cause of recurrent abdominal pain
Attacks are recurrent, stereotyped episodes of moderate-to-severe midline or periumbilical dull pain lasting hours (typically up to 72 hours) with completely symptom-free intervals
Associated features include anorexia, nausea, vomiting and pallor; the child often looks unwell and withdraws from normal activity
The pain is characteristically midline and poorly localised, the abdomen is normal on examination, and the child is entirely well between attacks
A personal or family history of migraine is common and many children later develop typical migraine headaches
Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3 criteria (at least five attacks of midline pain lasting 2-72 hours with at least two of anorexia, nausea, vomiting or pallor and no better explanation)
It remains a diagnosis of exclusion, so a careful history and examination are needed to exclude gastrointestinal, renal and surgical causes
Management mirrors migraine care with trigger avoidance, reassurance, acute symptomatic measures and migraine prophylaxis in frequent or severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Abdominal migraine is considered part of the migraine continuum, sharing mechanisms with migraine including trigeminovascular activation, dysregulation of the brain-gut axis and altered central pain processing. The same paroxysmal neuronal excitability and neuropeptide changes thought to drive migraine are expressed with the gut as the principal symptomatic target, producing episodic midline pain with autonomic accompaniments. There is strong familial and genetic overlap with migraine, and attacks are provoked by migraine-type triggers such as stress, fatigue, missed meals and certain foods.
additionalDifferentials: Functional abdominal pain and irritable bowel syndrome
Cyclical vomiting syndrome (a related episodic syndrome)
Intermittent obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus or recurrent intussusception, and recurrent appendicitis
Urinary tract infection or pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction
Inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease
additionalInvestigations: Thorough history including an attack diary and family history of migraine
Abdominal examination with growth and weight monitoring between attacks
Urinalysis to exclude a urinary tract cause
Basic bloods including full blood count, inflammatory markers and coeliac serology to exclude organic disease
Abdominal ultrasound if structural or renal pathology is suspected
Referral for further gastrointestinal evaluation such as endoscopy only if red flags are present
redFlags: Bilious vomiting or pain that is not midline or is localised away from the umbilicus
Weight loss, faltering growth or nocturnal waking with pain or diarrhoea
Gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting or signs of obstruction
Abnormal examination findings such as a mass, organomegaly or perianal disease
Fever, joint symptoms or other systemic features suggesting organic disease
reference.prognosis: Abdominal migraine is benign and self-limiting; attacks typically diminish over time and most children become symptom-free. A substantial proportion, however, develop migraine headaches during adolescence or adulthood.
pitfalls: Labelling pain as abdominal migraine before excluding organic gastrointestinal, renal or surgical disease
Failing to recognise the migraine link and so delaying appropriate migraine-directed management
Attributing the pain purely to psychological causes and missing the diagnosis
Missing bilious vomiting or faltering growth that signal an alternative diagnosis
Over-investigating a child with a typical, stereotyped presentation and a normal examination
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Reassure the family of the benign nature and identify and avoid triggers such as missed meals, poor sleep, dehydration, stress and specific dietary precipitants
Manage acute attacks supportively with rest in a quiet dark room, simple analgesia and an antiemetic, considering a nasal or oral triptan for severe attacks in older children
For frequent or disabling attacks, offer prophylaxis with agents used in paediatric migraine such as pizotifen, propranolol, cyproheptadine, flunarizine or topiramate
Encourage lifestyle regularity with consistent meals, adequate hydration and good sleep hygiene
Keep an attack diary to characterise frequency, triggers and treatment response
Follow up to monitor for evolution into typical migraine headache and re-evaluate if the pattern changes or red flags emerge
